$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)=\rho D_tu.$$

Substitute the first balance in [A1] into step 1.1 and apply [F5] to $\sigma$, using countable choice from [F6]. This yields
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\rho D_tu-\rho b-\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$

Every sufficiently small open ball $Q\Subset\Omega_t$ is such a material region: its inverse image under $\chi_t$ is a bounded $C^1$ region compactly contained in $B$. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant) and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Use SI units in a classical Cartesian inertial frame with absolute time; inertial changes have form $t^*=t+t_0$, $x^*=Qx+ct+d$, where $SO(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\det Q=1\}$, $c$ is a constant relative velocity in metres per second, and $d$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. Let $\sigma\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$ be Cauchy stress in pascals, with traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ for every outward Euclidean unit normal $n$. For every nonempty bounded open reference region $V$ whose closure is compact in $B$ and whose $C^1$ boundary is locally a graph with the region on one side, put $P_t=\chi_t(V)$. Adopt on each $P_t$ the material mass, linear-momentum and angular-momentum balances:

$$\int_{P_t}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The adopted traction representation is pointwise unique. The local momentum and stress-symmetry conclusions below hold on the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$; the larger $\mathcal O$ supplies ambient regularity only. $$\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b,$$

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

This is a conditional deduction in the smooth material model and asserts no extension to weak fields or vacuum.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. $$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Adopt the Axiom of Countable Choice, meaning that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. For $n\ge1$, use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue measure space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal L_n,\lambda_n)$, where $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ is the Caratheodory-measurable family for Lebesgue outer measure and $\lambda_n$ is that outer measure restricted to $\mathcal L_n$. The sigma-algebra and complete-measure assertions are the Lebesgue measure theorem under this axiom. For a Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, use the trace sigma-algebra $\mathcal L_E:=\{E\cap B:B\in\mathcal L_n\}$ and the measure $\lambda_E(A):=\lambda_n(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal L_E$; its countable additivity is inherited from $\lambda_n$. A map $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal L_E$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, where the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. For matrix-valued maps use their finite coordinate arrays. A property holds almost everywhere on $E$ when its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\lambda_E$-null set. Nonnegative integrals are suprema of nonnegative simple minorants; signed real integrals are the difference of the positive- and negative-part integrals when those parts are finite. Finite-dimensional integrals are taken componentwise.

Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Put $D:=\Omega\times[0,T)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ in spatial-first coordinates $(x,t)$. Both $D$ and $\Omega$ are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. Spatial integrals use $\lambda_\Omega$ from $\lambda_3$, and space-time integrals use $\lambda_D$ from $\lambda_4$. For a finite coordinate array $v$, set $\|v\|_1:=\sum_i|v_i|$, summing all entries for a matrix. A measurable field $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is locally integrable when $\int_K\|f\|_1\,d\lambda_E<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq E$. For $E=D$ the compact sets are taken in the relative topology, including those meeting $t=0$. Fields on $D$ are identified up to $\lambda_D$-almost-everywhere equality, and initial fields on $\Omega$ up to $\lambda_\Omega$-almost-everywhere equality. The slice $\Omega\times\{0\}$ is contained in a Lebesgue-null coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb R^4$; values of a space-time representative on that slice do not determine the separately prescribed initial field.

In the displayed weak identities, $\int_0^T\int_\Omega f\,dx\,dt$ denotes the joint integral of the zero extension of $f$ from $D$ with respect to $\lambda_4$.
